claim: Listening to radio drives people insane and to murder or suicide.
what_happened: The cases were people with existing psychosis who folded the new technology into their delusions; radio caused no rise in insanity.
lesson: When a new technology shows up inside a mental-health tragedy, it is usually the content of the delusion, not the cause; don't let anecdote set your product policy.

quotes.text: Insanity Induced by Wireless Blamed for Deaths by Bible Teacher.
quotes.speaker: The South Bend Tribune (unsigned)

quotes.text: FANCIED TORTURE BY RADIO WAVES CAUSES SUICIDE
quotes.speaker: Sioux City Journal (headline)

quotes.text: After hearing a radio announcer say that suicide once waa considered a virtue
quotes.speaker: Times Union (UP wire)

claim: Broadcast waves cause storms, floods, drought and freak weather.
what_happened: Meteorologists dismissed it at the time; broadcasting has no measurable effect on weather, and the claim resurfaced with every drought.
lesson: A credentialed person saying it does not make it physics; ask for the mechanism and the control group before you react.

quotes.text: The fast multiplying activities of the radio broadcasting stations were directly responsible for both the Florida and Vera Cruz hurricanes
quotes.speaker: Joaquin Gallo, director of Tacubaya Observatory (reported)

quotes.text: Excessive broadcasting of electric waves is causing freak weather all over the world.
quotes.speaker: Capt. W. H. Parker, commander of the Homeric

quotes.text: Peasants of the mountain regions near here have destroyed all their wireless sets in the belief that radio has attracted the unusually cold weather during the present summer.
quotes.speaker: AP wire, Nowy Sacz

claim: Radio waves kill birds, blotch skin and discolour drinking water.
what_happened: Each case had a mundane cause (Japanese-beetle spray for the birds, grounding wires on water pipes); radio waves at broadcast power do none of it.
lesson: Expect every unexplained harm in your users' lives to be blamed on the newest visible thing; have the boring explanation ready.

quotes.text: BUGS, NOT RADIO, KILLED BLACKBIRDS
quotes.speaker: Pittsburgh Post-Gazette (headline)

quotes.text: Radio already has been made the scapegoat for severe changes of climate and floors, but never was it accused until a few days ago of causing a person's face and body to acquire large blue splotches.
quotes.speaker: Honolulu Star-Bulletin (card)

claim: Concentrating on earphones gives women a wrinkled 'radio face'.
what_happened: No 'radio face' ever appeared; the worry vanished once loudspeakers replaced earphones.
lesson: Cosmetic fears about a new device usually track one awkward early form factor and die with it.

quotes.text: WOMEN IN ENGLAND FEAR "RADIO" FACE
quotes.speaker: The Ottawa Journal (headline)

quotes.text: Concentration at the Earphones Brings Wrinkles to the Brow
quotes.speaker: card subhead

claim: Late-night radio robs children and students of sleep and makes them laggards at school.
what_happened: Colleges banned dorm sets briefly; radio became normal, but the core worry (evening media displacing sleep) is now well evidenced for screens.
lesson: The displacement-of-sleep worry recurs with every evening medium and has real substance; design for bedtime rather than deny it.

quotes.text: Radio Blamed For Loss Of Sleep and Laggards In School Work, Report
quotes.speaker: Dayton Daily News (headline)

quotes.text: some college heads have actually forbidden the use of radio instruments in the campus dormitories
quotes.speaker: Israel Klein, NEA science editor

quotes.text: When It's Homework Or Radio to Child, Radio's the Winner!
quotes.speaker: Gladys Bevans

claim: A radio left on in the background stunts children's concentration and taste.
what_happened: Radio-as-background became universal; later research on background TV found it does fragment toddlers' play and reduce parent talk.
lesson: Ambient, always-on media has measurable costs for small children even when the content is harmless; quantity is its own variable.

quotes.text: An adult who unthinkingly allows a radio to run incessantly as a background to every home activity is hindering the sensitive child (or even a normal one) in developing concentration, discrimination and fineness of taste
quotes.speaker: unattributed (card)

quotes.text: Isn't how many hours' the radio is on also an important factor in what influence it has on children and family life?
quotes.speaker: Ruth Millett, NEA

claim: Blood-and-thunder radio programs will turn children into criminals.
what_happened: Networks moved crime shows later in the evening; the predicted delinquent generation did not appear and the fear moved straight on to comics and TV.
lesson: The fear attaches to whatever children love most this decade; it migrates on schedule, so build parental controls, not apologies.

quotes.text: radio programs would make American children more of a problem in the postwar world than the worst propaganda-corrupted youngsters in the Axis nations
quotes.speaker: Dorothy Gordon, Office of Civilian Defense

quotes.text: I'm against anything that glamorizes crime
quotes.speaker: Michael Riordan, San Francisco Chief of Police

quotes.text: I've been listening to too many radio programs, I guess.
quotes.speaker: Los Angeles cafe looter, reported by Bob Hope

claim: Free music on the radio will empty concert halls and cheapen music.
what_happened: Some subscribers did drop concerts, but radio vastly grew the audience for music and orchestras themselves went on air (NBC Symphony, 1937).
lesson: Incumbents who call a new channel a threat often end up as its best content supply; position to be carried, not displaced.

quotes.text: Music is no longer an exceptional sort of festive entertainment. It has been degraded to a common, everyday, matter-of-fact pleasure of life.
quotes.speaker: Kiel Philharmonic Society

quotes.text: RADIO MENACE LEADS ACTORS TO MOBILIZE
quotes.speaker: card headline

claim: Radio keeps people at home and spending on sets, ruining the wool, clothing and wider retail trade.
what_happened: Retail spending shifted, it did not collapse; consumer durables on credit became the engine of the decade.
lesson: When an incumbent blames a new product for its slump, check whether customers just moved their spending; a shift is not a loss.

quotes.text: RADIO BLAMED FOR POOR TRADE IN AUSTRALIA
quotes.speaker: Chicago Tribune Press Service (headline)

quotes.text: Radio Blamed for All Business Declines in New York, Is Complaint
quotes.speaker: Dayton Daily News (headline)

quotes.text: new in dustry to be a. boon instead of a bugaboo
quotes.speaker: Dayton Daily News

claim: Hearing sermons on the radio will empty the churches.
what_happened: US church attendance rose into the 1950s and radio became the main tool of evangelists and churches.
lesson: A broadcast of your thing is usually advertising for the live version; the institutions that feared radio later built empires on it.

quotes.text: Will Radio Kill Church Attendance?
quotes.speaker: Victoria Daily Times (Temple Talk headline)

claim: Radio will throw particular trades out of work, from blind piano tuners to the town crier.
what_happened: Narrow trades tied to the old way (town criers, home-piano tuning) did shrink sharply; broadcasting created far more jobs than it ended.
lesson: Job-loss warnings about specific trades are often right; the error is extrapolating them to the whole economy.

quotes.text: Blind Lose Jobs, Radio Blamed
quotes.speaker: card headline

quotes.text: TOWN-CRYING NOT WHAT IT USED TO BE; RADIO BLAMED
quotes.speaker: Santa Ana Register (headline)

claim: Broadcast major-league games will make fans ignore and kill local minor-league clubs.
what_happened: Minor leagues fell from 59 leagues in 1949 to about 20 by the early 1960s as broadcasts spread; they survived as major-league affiliates.
lesson: National broadcast does hollow out local mid-tier supply; the survivors became farm systems for the national winner.

quotes.text: Radio Blamed For Folding Of Minors
quotes.speaker: The Oil City Derrick (headline)

quotes.text: The president o a , minor baseball league who watched it dwindle from eight clubs to six. and finally wither and die
quotes.speaker: Whitney Martin, AP

claim: 'Radio mania' will alienate husbands from wives and break up homes.
what_happened: A handful of divorce suits cited radio; family listening around the set became the defining domestic scene of the 1930s.
lesson: The device that first looks like it isolates a family member often becomes the thing the family gathers around.

quotes.text: her husband paid more attention to his radio apparatus than to her
quotes.speaker: Associated Press, Minneapolis
quotes.publication: The Central New Jersey Home News

quotes.text: "Radio Craze" Blamed
quotes.speaker: card headline

quotes.text: Craze for Radio Causes Divorce
quotes.speaker: card headline

claim: The voices from a radio set are witchcraft, an instrument of the devil.
what_happened: In 1927 Polish villagers killed a radio owner as a witch; within a decade radio was in most homes and churches broadcast on it.
lesson: A technology that produces voices from nowhere triggers supernatural readings; explain the mechanism before strangers explain it for you.

quotes.text: smashed the “devil’s engine,” killed Its owner
quotes.speaker: Santa Ana Register (Warsaw dispatch)

quotes.text: RADIO AN INSTRUMENT OF DEVIL TO EX-MINISTER SUED BY WIFE
quotes.speaker: Daily News (headline)

quotes.text: EXPERTS MARVEL AS RADIO GHOST INVADES VILLAGE
quotes.speaker: Intelligencer Journal (headline)

claim: Loud radios will make neighbours' lives unbearable, driving fights, lawsuits and despair.
what_happened: Real conflicts and suits followed and cities wrote noise ordinances; the problem was managed by rules, not by abandoning radio.
lesson: Externalities that land on non-users are real and get regulated; price in the ordinance rather than fight it.

quotes.text: Sleep Killing Radio Is Cause of Suicide
quotes.speaker: The Eugene Guard (headline)

quotes.text: LOUD SPEAKING RADIO BLAMED FOR AN AFFRAY
quotes.speaker: The Times (headline)

quotes.text: A judge took the case under advisement after urging the owners to be reasonable in their use if the radio.
quotes.speaker: AP, Indianapolis

claim: Radios (later TVs) in cars will distract drivers and should be banned.
what_happened: Car radios became standard and were never banned; screens visible to drivers were restricted, and distracted driving became a recognised killer with phones.
lesson: Distraction fears are cheap to dismiss and expensive when they turn out to scale with the screen; separate audio from visual.

quotes.text: Automobile Radio Ban Proposals
quotes.speaker: card headline

quotes.text: The Auto Television Ban
quotes.speaker: card headline

claim: Commercial broadcasting will undermine education and crush local culture in favour of New York and Hollywood.
what_happened: National network culture did displace much local programming; the US answered decades later with public broadcasting (1967).
lesson: A centralising medium really does homogenise; the fix that worked was a parallel non-commercial channel, not a ban.

quotes.text: Commercial control of broadcasting under the American system threatens to crush out local culture in favor of "New Yorkism and Hollywoodism,"
quotes.speaker: Joy Elmer Morgan, National Congress of Parents and Teachers

quotes.text: Radio Threatens Culture, Morgan Tells P.-T. Meet
quotes.speaker: Star-Gazette (headline)

claim: Political speech on radio is dangerous and threatens the purity of elections.
what_happened: France required speeches to be pre-approved; radio powered both FDR's fireside chats and Coughlin and Goebbels, so the danger was real in the wrong hands.
lesson: A mass channel amplifies whoever masters it first; the political risk is real, so design for provenance rather than assume neutrality.

quotes.text: RADIO IN POLITICS PROVES DANGEROUS
quotes.speaker: Martin Codel (headline)

quotes.text: France has barred politics -from the radio industry.
quotes.speaker: Freeport Journal-Standard

quotes.text: Purity of Elections Violated by Radio?
quotes.speaker: card headline

claim: Fictional radio broadcasts will panic listeners into fleeing their homes.
what_happened: A few hundred did flee in Charleston in 1939; historians now argue newspapers, losing ad revenue to radio, inflated the 1938 War of the Worlds panic.
lesson: The incumbent medium's account of the new medium's harms deserves the same scepticism as the new medium's hype.

quotes.text: Radio Terror Play Routs Many Again
quotes.speaker: United Press (headline)

quotes.text: The play was interrupted seven times to sav it was all fiction.
quotes.speaker: United Press

claim: Radio transmissions disorient homing pigeons.
what_happened: Long dismissed; a 2014 Nature study found broadband electromagnetic noise does disrupt migratory birds' magnetic compass.
lesson: Some fringe fears turn out to have a narrow real core decades later; keep the door open to the specific mechanism.

quotes.text: Radio Waves Seem to Affect Homing Pigeons
quotes.speaker: card headline

claim: Claims that radio could carry the human voice across the Atlantic were absurd, and selling stock on them was fraud.
what_happened: Lee de Forest was tried for fraud in 1913 and acquitted; transatlantic radiotelephony worked by 1915 and became commercial service in 1927.
lesson: Prosecutors and regulators can call a real technology a scam; the honest test is the demo, not the incredulity.

quotes.text: Lee De Frost was put on trial for fraud after selling stock in his company developing long distance radio
quotes.speaker: card

claim: Crime and horror comics cause juvenile delinquency and teach children to kill.
what_happened: The 1954 Senate hearings led to the Comics Code, which gutted the industry; delinquency was not linked, and Wertham's case notes were later shown to be manipulated (Tilley, 2012).
lesson: A moral panic can win the regulatory fight decades before the evidence loses it; the Code shrank a whole industry on anecdotes.

quotes.text: An increase of violence in juvenile delinquency has gone hand in hand with the increased distribution of comic books featuring murder, torture and other violent crimes
quotes.speaker: Dr. Frederic Wertham, via Reader's Digest

quotes.text: Comic 'Murder Lesson' Costs Life of Boy 14
quotes.speaker: card headline

quotes.text: Then you think a child cannot in any way, shape, or manner, be hurt by anything that the child reads or sees?
quotes.speaker: Herbert Beaser, Senate Subcommittee chief counsel

claim: Colour comic magazines are a 'poisonous mushroom growth' of sex and horror corrupting a generation.
what_happened: Comics became mainstream culture and later classroom texts; the attack was led in part by a children's-book author and literary editor whose own market comics competed with.
lesson: Check what the loudest critic sells; the 1940 broadside came from a children's-book author defending his own shelf.

quotes.text: Virtually every child in America is reading color "comic" magazines a poisonous mushroom growth of the last two years.
quotes.speaker: Sterling North, Chicago Daily News

quotes.text: Parents and teachers must join now in a crusade against comic books
quotes.speaker: Rev. Louis A. Ronglone, NJ Catholic Library Association

quotes.text: Comic books were named "unfunny funnies"
quotes.speaker: Indianapolis Star

claim: Brightly coloured comics strain children's eyes and over-excite their nerves.
what_happened: No eye damage or nervous disorder was ever traced to comics.
lesson: Physical-harm claims are often a respectable wrapper for a taste objection; ask what the critic would say if the harm were disproved.

quotes.text: Comic books are too brightly colored and are apt to strain children's eyes
quotes.speaker: Coshocton PTA mothers' round table

quotes.text: Comic Books Injurious to Children, Mothers Decide
quotes.speaker: The Coshocton Tribune (headline)

claim: 'Comic book addiction' crowds out real books and wrecks children's reading.
what_happened: Studies found comic readers read as much or more; graphic novels entered libraries and curricula.
lesson: A format that looks like a lesser version of reading is often an on-ramp to it; librarians who resisted comics later shelved them.

quotes.text: Does your daughter spurn the Christmas books you so Carefully selected? Comics again.
quotes.speaker: Richmond Barbour PhD, California Congress of Parents and Teachers

quotes.text: Good Books Called Answer To Comic Book Addiction
quotes.speaker: Albuquerque Journal (headline)

claim: Comics carry fascist or un-American (or Red) ideology into children's minds.
what_happened: No propaganda effect materialised; superhero comics became America's most exported cultural form.
lesson: Accusations that a popular medium is a foreign ideological plot track the geopolitics of the day, not the medium.

quotes.text: The Press: Are Comics Fascist?
quotes.speaker: TIME (card headline)

quotes.text: one wonders why no one has suspected the American comic-book industry of being a Red Plot
quotes.speaker: Marghanita Laski, review of Seduction of the Innocent

claim: Moving-picture shows corrupt children's morals and teach them crime.
what_happened: Cities licensed and censored theatres and Hollywood adopted the Hays Code; film became the century's dominant art and no corrupted generation appeared.
lesson: Early, cheap, unregulated venues attract the worst content and the loudest critics; quality and respectability arrive with scale.

quotes.text: SAY PICTURE SHOWS CORRUPT CHILDREN
quotes.speaker: The New York Times (headline)

quotes.text: Vile Moving Pictures Corrupting the Morals of Countless Children
quotes.speaker: card headline

quotes.text: EFFECT OF MOVIES ON CHILD FOUND BAD
quotes.speaker: card headline

claim: Watching movies gives children 'moving picture eye' and damages eyesight.
what_happened: Early flicker did cause eyestrain, but faster frame rates fixed it and no lasting damage was found; oculists at the time expected eyes to adjust.
lesson: Early-version discomfort gets read as permanent harm; ship the fix and the health scare usually dies with the defect.

quotes.text: MOVING PICTURE EYE NEW FLAW IN RACE
quotes.speaker: Delaware County Daily Times (headline)

quotes.text: This does not mean that the eyesight of the world is threatened.
quotes.speaker: St. Louis Post-Dispatch

claim: Films weaken the mind of the moviegoer and spread modern ills.
what_happened: No cognitive decline followed; film criticism and film schools treated cinema as an intellectual art within a generation.
lesson: 'It rots the brain' is the oldest review of any new medium; the medium outlives the review.

quotes.text: SAYS FILMS WEAKEN MIND OF MOVIE GOER
quotes.speaker: card headline

quotes.text: Movies, Radio Blamed For Many Modern Ills
quotes.speaker: card headline

quotes.text: Present War Laid to German Youth
quotes.speaker: card headline

claim: Talking pictures are a novelty that will not replace silent films.
what_happened: Within two years nearly all Hollywood output was sound; silent film was finished by 1930.
lesson: Executives invested in the current format are the least reliable judges of whether its successor is a fad.

quotes.text: Talking motion pictures are novelties and only reproductions of appropriate sounds are capable of enhancing screen dramas
quotes.speaker: Joseph M. Schenck, President of United Artists (reported)

quotes.text: 'TALKIES' JUST A FAD, SAYS JOSEPH SCHENCK
quotes.speaker: card headline

claim: Colour adds nothing to motion pictures.
what_happened: Colour became standard by the late 1960s once costs fell.
lesson: 'What's the point?' about a richer format usually means 'not at this price'; watch the cost curve, not the shrug.

quotes.text: What's the point of color films?
quotes.speaker: card headline

claim: Picture shows are killing the dime novel.
what_happened: Dime novels did vanish in the 1920s; the thrill moved to film and pulp magazines.
lesson: A new medium often kills a specific format outright while the appetite behind it thrives; own the appetite, not the format.

quotes.text: Movie Shows Blamed Tor Disappearance Of Dime Novels
quotes.speaker: The Standard Union (headline)

quotes.text: When little Johnny feels like reading a dime novel nowadays he goes to a picture show for almost the same price
quotes.speaker: a Columbus bookseller

claim: Home video exposes children to sadistic 'video nasties' they can replay at will.
what_happened: Britain passed the Video Recordings Act 1984; the survey behind the panic was later discredited and many banned films were re-released uncut.
lesson: On-demand control over content is what makes the new format valuable and what makes it frightening; expect ratings regimes, not bans, to settle it.

quotes.text: children prefer home videos to the cinema or television because they can stop the film and re-run the most blood-thirsty and violent sequences
quotes.speaker: Evening Standard

claim: Genetically altered foods are unsafe and should carry warning signs.
what_happened: Scientific bodies found approved GM foods as safe as conventional ones; GM crops became most US corn and soy while labelling fights continued.
lesson: Fiction shapes the public's model of a new technology before any data does; the industry that ignores the story loses the framing.

quotes.text: People in the field are very nervous about the negative impact of Jurassic Park
quotes.speaker: Thomas Montville, Rutgers University

quotes.text: The true purpose of the signs," she said, "is not to inform consumers, but to scare them.
quotes.speaker: Laurel Nelson, National Food Processors Association

claim: Television is an addiction comparable to drugs, especially for children.
what_happened: TV viewing rose to 4+ hours a day and displacement of reading and socialising was real; 'addiction' stayed contested and the panic moved to games and phones.
lesson: Heavy-use worries about a beloved medium are usually partly right about time displaced and wrong about catastrophe; measure hours, not headlines.

quotes.text: The kid becomes agitated and nervous and does not know how to fill his time,
quotes.speaker: Dr. Gordon S. Livingston, child psychiatrist

quotes.text: 93 of 120 families spurned an offer of $500 to turn off the set for a month
quotes.speaker: Boston Globe (Detroit Free Press study)

quotes.text: Childrens Addiction to TV has become an alarming problem.
quotes.speaker: Valley Times (Dr. Isidore Ziferstein series)

claim: Violent TV can make a child kill ('television intoxication').
what_happened: A Miami jury rejected the 'television addiction' murder defence in under two hours; research found small aggression effects but no link to homicide.
lesson: Courts and data separate small measurable effects from causal blame; don't build policy on the defence lawyer's version.

quotes.text: 'Television addiction' no defense for murder
quotes.speaker: The Pocono Record (UPI headline)

quotes.text: Zamora killed an elderly widow in a moment of insanity in which he felt he was playing out a television drama.
quotes.speaker: UPI

claim: Seeing-at-a-distance means nobody will have any privacy any more.
what_happened: Broadcast TV posed no privacy threat, but networked cameras in every phone and doorbell later made the joke a policy question.
lesson: A privacy fear that is wrong for the first form of a technology can be right for its networked descendant.

quotes.text: Will Envisions Some Troubles of Television
quotes.speaker: Wisconsin State Journal (headline)

quotes.text: no privacy any more
quotes.speaker: Will Rogers

claim: Home television will destroy the movie-theatre business.
what_happened: US weekly attendance roughly halved through the 1950s, but studios survived by making TV content and widescreen spectacle.
lesson: A substitute that removes friction (parking, sitters) wins the casual customer; incumbents survive by supplying it and selling what home can't.

quotes.text: There is no parking problem, no baby sitting expense, and one can enjoy programs completely relaxed.
quotes.speaker: The Bee (editorial)

quotes.text: TV had better watch out and everything is going to be ginger-peachy
quotes.speaker: The York Dispatch

claim: 3D movies are a passing gimmick with no real future.
what_happened: The 1953 boom collapsed within two years, and the 2009 revival faded again by the late 2010s.
lesson: Sceptics are sometimes right: a format that adds friction (glasses, headaches) for marginal gain fades no matter how hard the industry pushes it.

quotes.text: experts are reported to be skeptical over the future of 3D movies
quotes.speaker: Hal Humphrey

quotes.text: flatties" are out, deepies are in
quotes.speaker: The York Dispatch

claim: Television is a waste of people's time.
what_happened: TV became the dominant leisure activity for half a century; time-use studies confirm it displaced reading and civic life, as Putnam later argued.
lesson: 'Waste of time' critiques are usually right about displacement and wrong about whether people will choose it anyway.

quotes.text: Archbishop of Canterbury Thinks TV Is Waste of People's Time; He Has No Set
quotes.speaker: Hal Humphrey (subhead)

claim: Remote controls make viewers lazy and shorten attention spans.
what_happened: Remotes became universal; channel-surfing did change programming toward faster hooks, a pattern later amplified by feeds.
lesson: Each cut in friction changes what content wins; expect the format to adapt to the faster thumb.

quotes.text: Remote Controls are Lazy!
quotes.speaker: card headline

quotes.text: Remote Control Shortened Attention Spans
quotes.speaker: card headline

claim: The computer's landslide election forecast must be a mistake.
what_happened: UNIVAC predicted 438 electoral votes for Eisenhower on 3 million votes; he won 442. CBS and its own operators sat on it because everyone expected a close race.
lesson: When a model contradicts the consensus, the humans around it are the bottleneck; decide in advance what result would make you publish.

quotes.text: They decided UNIVAC must have made a mistake somewhere along the line, so the prediction was not televised.
quotes.speaker: Star-Gazette

quotes.text: It said General Eisenhower would get 438 electoral votes and Governor Stevenson would get 93. The actual result was 442 to 89.
quotes.speaker: Star-Gazette

claim: The crossword craze is an addiction wasting time and interfering with work and training.
what_happened: Professors banned them from classrooms in 1924; crosswords became a respectable daily habit and are now promoted for cognitive health.
lesson: Today's time-wasting craze can become tomorrow's prestige habit; the New York Times mocked crosswords, then made them a core product.

quotes.text: a really serious indictment of the craze is uttered by the president of an athletic union who asserts that it interferes with the training of
quotes.speaker: press comment

quotes.text: Too Many Puzzles.
quotes.speaker: Harrisburg Telegraph

claim: Pinball machines are gambling devices that addict men and ruin families.
what_happened: Many machines did pay out and were raided and banned (NYC 1942-1976); once payouts were separated from play, bans were lifted and pinball became nostalgic.
lesson: The fear was right about the payout mechanic and wrong about the game; separating the two is what saved the product.

quotes.text: for many years I have endured endless anxiety because my husband can't leave the machines alone.
quotes.speaker: letter to Mary Marker

quotes.text: the machines were illegal gambling devices if the owners did not hold the $250 federal excise stamp
quotes.speaker: UPI

claim: Arcade games like Pac-Man and Space Invaders addict young people, and arcades should be banned.
what_happened: Towns banned arcades in the early 1980s; games became the largest entertainment industry, while the WHO recognised gaming disorder in a small minority (2019).
lesson: Addiction fears are partly right for a minority and wrong for the mass; build for the minority without letting it define the product.

quotes.text: the force for evil which can arise among young people from addiction to 'space invader' machines.
quotes.speaker: George Foulkes MP, House of Commons

quotes.text: playing these games actually is very similar to gambling
quotes.speaker: Pauline Carlson, letter

quotes.text: Pac-Man Banned In Massachusetts Town
quotes.speaker: AP headline

claim: Games like Grand Theft Auto make players violent.
what_happened: Youth violence fell as game sales rose; the Supreme Court struck down California's sales ban (2011) and the APA (2020) found no link to violent crime.
lesson: Aggregate trends are the cheapest test of a harm claim: if the thing tripled and the harm fell, the causal story is weak.

quotes.text: Game Over - How 'Grand Theft Auto' is affecting us
quotes.speaker: card headline

claim: Dungeons & Dragons drives teenagers to suicide, murder and the occult.
what_happened: A CDC review found no link; D&D outlived the panic and boomed again in the 2010s as a social game.
lesson: Grieving parents plus one psychiatrist can launch a national campaign; the product survived by outlasting it, not out-arguing it.

quotes.text: Group Of Worried Parents Links Suicides Slayings To Fantasy Game
quotes.speaker: Billy Bowles, Knight-Ridder (headline)

quotes.text: The game is full of human sacrifice
quotes.speaker: quoted critic

quotes.text: 'Dungeons & Dragons' addict's suicide gives rise to a lawsuit
quotes.speaker: Michael Isikoff, Washington Post

claim: Pokemon cards are a gateway to gambling for five-year-olds.
what_happened: No generation of gamblers followed, but random-pack mechanics later got regulated as gambling-like in video-game loot boxes (Belgium 2018).
lesson: Randomised rewards sold to children are where the gambling critique keeps landing; keep the randomness away from the payment.

quotes.text: Now 5 and 6-year-olds are buying Pokemon and it begs the question: is this the gateway to gambling?
quotes.speaker: Valerie Lorenz, compulsive-gambling researcher

claim: Children who read newspapers will learn too much and become dissatisfied with home.
what_happened: Newspapers became a standard tool of literacy and civics; the same objection recurs with every window onto the wider world.
lesson: Some resistance is really a fear that users will outgrow the status quo; that is a sign of value, not harm.

quotes.text: The objection was, that his children would learn too much that they would become dissatisfied with home
quotes.speaker: York Gazette (reprinted article)

quotes.text: Should Young Children Read Newspapers
quotes.speaker: Los Angeles Herald (headline)

claim: Bulky Sunday papers keep men from church.
what_happened: Sunday editions became the most-read papers of the week while church attendance rose into the 1950s.
lesson: Competing for the same hour is not the same as destroying an institution; both can grow.

quotes.text: That reason is Sunday newspapers.
quotes.speaker: letter to the editor

quotes.text: NEWSPAPERS BLAMED. An Assertion That They Are a Power for Evil, Not Good.
quotes.speaker: The Times (headline)

claim: The 'newspaper habit' is a new vice feeding a love of the sensational instead of real reading.
what_happened: Mass newspapers did run on sensationalism (yellow journalism), but they also built the informed public; the vice framing faded.
lesson: Critiques of the incentive (sensationalism sells) tend to be right; critiques of the habit itself tend to be wrong.

quotes.text: We have heard all about the drink habit, the tobacco habit and the opium habit
quotes.speaker: Los Angeles Times editorial

quotes.text: "THE NEWSPAPER HABIT."
quotes.speaker: Los Angeles Times (headline)

claim: Reading the paper at the dinner table shuts the family out.
what_happened: The table newspaper became a cliché, and the same complaint now attaches to phones, with some evidence that devices at meals reduce conversation.
lesson: The isolation complaint follows whatever portable screen is at the table; it is about attention etiquette, not the device.

quotes.text: Mr. Married Man, are you in the habit of reading at the dinner table? If you do, you are not treating your family fairly.
quotes.speaker: card (International News Service column)

claim: Edison's electric light is impractical and a bad investment against gas.
what_happened: Electric light displaced gas lighting within a generation; gas companies' resistance only delayed it.
lesson: When monopolies set up 'cabals' against a new energy source, that is evidence it threatens them, not that it fails.

quotes.text: feel that electricity will break down their power, and are setting up cabals against it.
quotes.speaker: Pall Mall Gazette Paris correspondent

quotes.text: Cost complaints and warning to investors
quotes.speaker: card headline

quotes.text: City Council Votes Against Electric Light
quotes.speaker: card headline

claim: High-voltage alternating current is deadly and unsafe for city distribution.
what_happened: AC was dangerous at high voltage, but insulation and underground wiring made it safe; Edison, invested in DC, lost and AC became the world standard.
lesson: A competitor's safety warning can be both true and self-serving; the winner fixes the danger instead of conceding the point.

quotes.text: attempts to cast discredit upon the converter or alternating current system
quotes.speaker: Pittsburgh Daily Post, on Edison's North American Review article

quotes.text: WESTIXGllOUSE TO EDISON. THE ALTERNATING SYSTEM IS DEFENDED.
quotes.speaker: Pittsburgh Daily Post (headline, OCR)

claim: Electric light makes the shadows darker, helping thieves and hidden gambling.
what_happened: Street lighting spread everywhere and is generally associated with less crime, not more.
lesson: A new thing's side effect gets noticed before its main effect; measure the net, not the shadow.

quotes.text: those in the shadow were correspondingly dark
quotes.speaker: The Indianapolis News

quotes.text: ELECTRIC LIGHT BLAMED
quotes.speaker: Buffalo Morning Express (subhead)
quotes.publication: Buffalo Morning Express and Illustrated Buffalo Express

claim: Artificial light keeps people up late and hooked on night life.
what_happened: Electric light became universal; circadian research now shows evening light exposure does delay sleep, the same mechanism blamed on screens.
lesson: Some 'lifestyle' fears are physiological and get confirmed a century later; worth designing night modes early.

quotes.text: Professor laments electric lights keeping people up and addicted to ‘night life’
quotes.speaker: card headline

quotes.text: Too Much Artificial Light
quotes.speaker: card headline

claim: Electric appliances will make housewives lazy and fat.
what_happened: Appliances cut housework hours sharply and are linked by economists to the rise in women's paid work.
lesson: 'It will make people lazy' usually describes freed time that gets reallocated to something more valuable.

quotes.text: "Lazy and Fat" + Liberation
quotes.speaker: card note

claim: The theatre debases young men and undoes a Christian upbringing.
what_happened: Theatre became respectable education; by 1964 drama teachers were defending it as building poise and literacy.
lesson: Moral objections to an art form fade as it gets institutions; schools end up teaching what churches once forbade.

quotes.text: The moral principles which have cost a Christian mother months of care are banished in an hour.
quotes.speaker: The Lutheran Observer

quotes.text: TOO MUCH THEATRE.
quotes.speaker: The Dayton Herald (headline)

quotes.text: Theatre Doesn't Corrupt Children
quotes.speaker: Calgary Herald (CP headline)

claim: Personal headphones tune people out of life and usher in an age of isolation.
what_happened: Headphones became universal (AirPods); the isolation argument fed straight into 'Bowling Alone' and now smartphones, without a clear verdict.
lesson: A private-experience device will always be read as antisocial; the market chooses it anyway, so design the social on-ramp.

quotes.text: Walkman Earphones: Mind-Altering Devices
quotes.speaker: Bob Greene (headline)

quotes.text: Headsets tune out life itself
quotes.speaker: card headline

quotes.text: isolation is a result of plugging in
quotes.speaker: card headline

claim: Wearing headphones on the street or while driving is dangerous and should be illegal.
what_happened: Woodbridge, NJ banned headphones for drivers and pedestrians in 1982; some states still restrict them while driving, and distracted walking is a measured risk.
lesson: Local bans on a popular device rarely stick, but the safety point often survives as a narrow rule; argue for the narrow rule.

quotes.text: Headphone Wearer Arrested in New Jersey
quotes.speaker: card headline

quotes.text: Personal Stereo Comes Under Attack
quotes.speaker: card headline

claim: A moon expedition would be a terrible waste of money.
what_happened: Apollo landed in 1969 at about $25bn; polls showed most Americans doubted it was worth it, and its payoff (technology, prestige) is still argued.
lesson: Moonshot cost critiques are unfalsifiable at decision time; the defensible case names the spillovers in advance.

quotes.text: The moon expedition would be a terrible waste of money
quotes.speaker: card headline

claim: Man has not really set foot on the moon; it was staged.
what_happened: The landings are confirmed by returned samples, retroreflectors and independent tracking; the hoax belief persisted in a minority.
lesson: Some people will deny a breakthrough happened at all; evidence that others can independently check is the only durable answer.

quotes.text: Some Believe Moon- Landing Is a Hoax
quotes.speaker: Lee Mueller, NEA (headline)

claim: People don't want to be seen on calls, so video phones won't catch on.
what_happened: Right for 30 years (Picturephone, 1980s freeze-frame phones flopped); wrong once video was free and default (FaceTime 2010, Zoom 2020).
lesson: 'People don't want it' is often really 'not at this price and quality'; the behaviour objection held until the cost hit zero.

quotes.text: The issue is behavior,
quotes.speaker: A. Michael Noll, USC, former AT&T product planner

quotes.text: Seeing somebody almost destroys the intimacy
quotes.speaker: A. Michael Noll

claim: Cheap copying machines flood organisations with paper nobody can read.
what_happened: Office paperwork did explode with each copying technology (typewriter, Xerox, email); productivity grew anyway, at a real coordination cost.
lesson: When producing documents gets cheap, reading them becomes the bottleneck; the value moves to whoever filters.

quotes.text: One of the things wrong with this country may be too many typewriters.
quotes.speaker: The Daily News editorial

quotes.text: Somebody has to read all the papers typed, and find a use for them, or at least a place to put them.
quotes.speaker: The Daily News editorial

claim: Tall lit monuments kill migrating birds in large numbers.
what_happened: The Smithsonian's Ridgway was right: building and window collisions now kill an estimated 365-988 million birds a year in the US (Loss et al., 2014).
lesson: Not every early warning is a panic; the ones grounded in counted bodies, like Ridgway's birds, tend to hold.

quotes.text: which are killed in large numbers by 'flying against the Statue of Liberty
quotes.speaker: Berkshire County Eagle, on Prof. Ridgway of the Smithsonian

claim: Mandatory flu masks let criminals hide their faces and drive a crime wave.
what_happened: No mask crime wave was documented in 1918-19 or during COVID-19 masking.
lesson: Any privacy-giving tool will be blamed for crime by police first; ask for the before-and-after numbers.

quotes.text: FLU MASKS CAUSE MOST OF CRIME SAYS SACRAMENTAN
quotes.speaker: Bakersfield Morning Echo (headline)

claim: Photographs of nude paintings are obscene and should be seized.
what_happened: A Philadelphia court rebuffed Comstock; art reproductions circulated freely, though Comstock laws persisted for decades.
lesson: Cheap reproduction moves art out of galleries and into censors' reach; courts tend to side with the art once it is named as art.

quotes.text: If he is upheld in his stupid crusade
quotes.speaker: The Lancaster Examiner, on Anthony Comstock

claim: Abolitionists are fanatics waging war on religion and the Constitution.
what_happened: Slavery was abolished by the 13th Amendment in 1865; the 'fanatics' became the moral consensus.
lesson: Calling a reform movement 'fanatics' is a description of how far ahead of consensus it is, not of whether it is wrong.

quotes.text: the notorious Garrison
quotes.speaker: New York Daily Herald special reporter

claim: Painless surgery is a chimera that cannot be achieved.
what_happened: Ether anaesthesia was demonstrated in Boston in 1846, seven years later, and spread worldwide within months.
lesson: Experts declaring a long-sought goal impossible are often closest to being overtaken by it.

claim: A talking machine is impossible, so Edison's phonograph must be a trick.
what_happened: Edison demonstrated it in person and the phonograph founded the recorded-music industry.
lesson: A live demo ends a 'that's impossible' argument faster than any paper; put the thing in the sceptic's hands.

quotes.text: Thomas Edison Proves Cynic Wrong in Person
quotes.speaker: card headline

claim: Beepers are the drug dealer's tool and must be banned in schools.
what_happened: Dealers did use pagers and many schools banned them; the bans faded as mobile phones became universal and schools moved to managing, not banning, devices.
lesson: Early criminal adopters taint a device; the stigma lasts only until ordinary users outnumber them.

quotes.text: Schools Responding to Beeper, Tool of Today's Drug Dealer, by Banning It
quotes.speaker: card headline

quotes.text: BEEPER BAN IN SCHOOLS URGED
quotes.speaker: card headline

claim: Machines are creating permanent mass unemployment that economists refuse to see.
what_happened: Depression-era mass unemployment ended with demand, not with fewer machines; displacement of specific workers was real while total employment grew.
lesson: Technology moves jobs faster than it removes them in aggregate; the pain is local and real, the apocalypse is not.

quotes.text: How the Economists Fool Themselves
quotes.speaker: card headline

claim: The flood of news and stimulation ends reflection and independent thought.
what_happened: The worry recurs with every medium (newspapers, radio, TV, internet); attention fragmentation is real, a collapse of thought is not evident.
lesson: 'The end of reflection' has been announced every generation; build tools that create space to think rather than argue the trend.

quotes.text: The End of Reflection
quotes.speaker: card headline

quotes.text: FAILURE TO THINK CALLED DAY'S PERIL
quotes.speaker: card headline

claim: Widespread encryption will shield criminals and terrorists from law enforcement.
what_happened: The 1990s crypto wars ended with strong encryption legal and ubiquitous (HTTPS, Signal); criminals do use it, and 'going dark' disputes continue.
lesson: Governments lose fights against math that protects commerce; the useful position is building lawful access around it, not against it.

quotes.text: The key issue for the Net is not the smut, it is the use of encryption
quotes.speaker: card headline

claim: Jitney drivers are unsafe, unfair competition and must be curbed.
what_happened: Streetcar companies pushed licensing and bonding laws that wiped out jitneys by about 1920; the model returned a century later as Uber and Lyft.
lesson: Incumbents can regulate a new transport model out of existence for a century; the demand waits for a technology that makes enforcement impossible.

quotes.text: Time to Curb Jitneurs
quotes.speaker: card headline
